:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Find the expression that gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$$
\displaystyle x=t, \, y=\ln{(\cos{t})}
$$
from $t=0$ to $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ (see graph below).

![](images/48/48de26c11ae08afb45ec19ee56e770f7418f9be2afb8ee7dd46a0d1136cb125b.png)
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \sqrt{ \left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2 + \left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2}\:\textrm{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡t))=-\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{(1)}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{tan}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{1+{tan}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{sec}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sec}⁡t\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$$
\displaystyle x = 1 + \sin (4t), y = 4\cos (t)
$$
from $t = 0$ to $t = 2$?

![](images/80/80577a585741748702b61596db84983592ecbc6c01fca78af033bf82dbe62ad2.png)

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$$
\displaystyle x={e}^{t},\,y={e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t
$$
from $t=-3$ to $t=1$ (shown above)?
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)={e}^{t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{1}\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+{e}^{2t}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{1}{e}^{t}\sqrt{1+{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{1}{e}^{t}\sqrt{2+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$$
\displaystyle x=t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t),\,y=1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)
$$
from $t=2$ to $t=5$ ?
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))=1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{5}\sqrt{(1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{2}+(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{5}\sqrt{1+4\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+4{cos}^{2}⁡(t)+4{sin}^{2}⁡(2t)}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$$
\displaystyle x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-1,\,y=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+2
$$
from $t=0$ to $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ ?
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-1) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\cdot 3 \\  & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+2) \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot 2 \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(6\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))^{2}+(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{36{cos}^{2}⁡(3t)+16{sin}^{2}⁡(2t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡(3t)+4{sin}^{2}⁡(2t)}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$$
\displaystyle x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t),\,y=t-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)
$$
from $t=0$ to $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ ?
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))^{2}+(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡(t)+{sin}^{2}⁡(t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+1+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+1+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{2+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\displaystyle x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=8t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=8-\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(8-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+64-16\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{10{sin}^{2}⁡t-16\operatorname{sin}⁡t+64}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$
